name: SQL & Data
title: Data Wrangler
blurb: Every target role needs data skills: consultants analyse client data in Excel and SQL, and SAP and Murex/Calypso projects live on queries, reconciliations, batch jobs and test evidence.

chapters.title: SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY
chapters.read: A free interactive SQL tutorial's first lessons (e.g. on SQLite or PostgreSQL): SELECT columns, WHERE with AND/OR/IN/BETWEEN/LIKE, IS NULL, ORDER BY ASC/DESC, LIMIT, and the logical order in which a query is evaluated.
chapters.produce: Load a 50-row CSV of your own expenses into SQLite and write 15 queries answering real questions (e.g. 'all food spending over ¥1,000 in May, largest first').

quiz.q:
Table emp:
id | name | dept  | salary
1  | Aiko | Sales | 300
2  | Ben  | Sales | 450
3  | Chen | IT    | 500
4  | Dai  | IT    | 350
5  | Emi  | HR    | 400

How many rows does this query return?
SELECT * FROM emp WHERE salary > 350 AND dept <> 'HR';
quiz.ex: Salaries above 350 are Ben 450, Chen 500 and Emi 400; Emi is in HR, so 2 rows remain.

quiz.q:
Table emp:
id | name | dept  | salary
1  | Aiko | Sales | 300
2  | Ben  | Sales | 450
3  | Chen | IT    | 500
4  | Dai  | IT    | 350
5  | Emi  | HR    | 400

Which query lists the names of IT employees, highest salary first?
opts: SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT' ORDER BY salary ASC;
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT' ORDER BY salary DESC;
SELECT name FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC WHERE dept = 'IT';
SELECT name FROM emp HAVING dept = 'IT' ORDER BY salary;
quiz.ex: WHERE must come before ORDER BY, and DESC sorts from highest to lowest.

quiz.q: A column bonus contains NULL for some rows. Which condition returns exactly those rows?
opts: WHERE bonus = NULL
WHERE bonus = 0
WHERE bonus IS NULL
WHERE bonus = ''
quiz.ex: NULL means unknown, so 'bonus = NULL' is never true; SQL uses IS NULL.

quiz.q:
Table emp:
id | name | dept  | salary
1  | Aiko | Sales | 300
2  | Ben  | Sales | 450
3  | Chen | IT    | 500
4  | Dai  | IT    | 350
5  | Emi  | HR    | 400

What value does this query return?
SELECT SUM(salary) FROM emp WHERE dept IN ('Sales', 'HR');
In which logical order is a simple query with FROM, WHERE, SELECT and ORDER BY evaluated?
opts: FROM, WHERE, SELECT, ORDER BY
SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY
ORDER BY, FROM, WHERE, SELECT
WHERE, FROM, ORDER BY, SELECT
quiz.ex: Rows are taken FROM tables, filtered by WHERE, columns are computed in SELECT, and the result is sorted last.

quiz.q: Which condition matches names that start with the letter A?
opts: WHERE name LIKE '%A'
WHERE name = 'A*'
WHERE name LIKE '_A'
WHERE name LIKE 'A%'
quiz.ex: % matches any number of characters after A. '%A' would mean 'ends with A', and '_A' means exactly one character followed by A.

chapters.title: JOINs
chapters.read: The JOIN lessons of a free SQL tutorial: INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER and CROSS joins, join keys, table aliases, finding unmatched rows, and the difference between filtering in ON and in WHERE.
chapters.produce: Create customer, order and product tables in SQLite and write 10 join queries, including 'customers with no orders' and 'orders whose customer is missing', checking each row count by hand.

quiz.q:
Table customers:
id | name
1  | Aoki
2  | Baba
3  | Chiba

Table orders:
id | cust_id | amount
10 | 1       | 100
11 | 1       | 200
12 | 2       | 50
13 | 4       | 70

How many rows does this query return?
SELECT * FROM customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON o.cust_id = c.id;
quiz.ex: Orders 10 and 11 match Aoki, order 12 matches Baba; order 13 has no customer 4, and Chiba has no orders. 3 rows.

quiz.q:
Table customers:
id | name
1  | Aoki
2  | Baba
3  | Chiba

Table orders:
id | cust_id | amount
10 | 1       | 100
11 | 1       | 200
12 | 2       | 50
13 | 4       | 70

How many rows does this query return?
SELECT * FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.cust_id = c.id;
quiz.ex: Every customer is kept: Aoki 2 rows, Baba 1 row, Chiba 1 row with NULL order columns. 4 rows.

quiz.q:
Table customers:
id | name
1  | Aoki
2  | Baba
3  | Chiba

Table orders:
id | cust_id | amount
10 | 1       | 100
11 | 1       | 200
12 | 2       | 50
13 | 4       | 70

Which query finds customers who have no orders?
opts: SELECT c.name FROM customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON o.cust_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;
SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.cust_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NOT NULL;
SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.cust_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;
SELECT c.name FROM customers c CROSS JOIN orders o;
quiz.ex: A LEFT JOIN keeps customers without a match and fills order columns with NULL; filtering on o.id IS NULL keeps only those.

quiz.q:
Table customers:
id | name
1  | Aoki
2  | Baba
3  | Chiba

Table orders:
id | cust_id | amount
10 | 1       | 100
11 | 1       | 200
12 | 2       | 50
13 | 4       | 70

How many rows does this query return?
SELECT * FROM customers c FULL OUTER JOIN orders o ON o.cust_id = c.id;
quiz.ex: 3 matched rows + Chiba (no order) + order 13 (no customer) = 5.

quiz.q:
Table customers:
id | name
1  | Aoki
2  | Baba
3  | Chiba

Table orders:
id | cust_id | amount
10 | 1       | 100
11 | 1       | 200
12 | 2       | 50
13 | 4       | 70

How many rows does SELECT * FROM customers CROSS JOIN orders; return?
quiz.ex: A cross join pairs every customer with every order: 3 × 4 = 12.

quiz.q: A query uses customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.cust_id = c.id and then WHERE o.amount > 100. What is the effect?
opts: Customers without orders disappear, because their NULL amount fails the WHERE test, so it behaves like an INNER JOIN
All customers are still returned, with NULL for small orders
The query fails with a syntax error
Only customers without orders are returned
quiz.ex: To keep unmatched customers, put the condition in the ON clause instead: ON o.cust_id = c.id AND o.amount > 100.

chapters.title: GROUP BY and HAVING
chapters.read: The aggregation lessons of a free SQL tutorial: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, COUNT(DISTINCT), GROUP BY with one or more columns, HAVING, and how NULLs affect aggregates.
chapters.produce: Using a public sales sample dataset in SQLite, produce a monthly sales report by region with totals, averages and order counts, and a list of regions whose sales fell below a threshold using HAVING.

quiz.q:
Table sales:
region | rep | amount
East   | A   | 100
East   | B   | 300
West   | C   | 200
West   | C   | 100
North  | D   | 50

How many rows does this query return?
SELECT region, SUM(amount) FROM sales GROUP BY region HAVING SUM(amount) > 150;
quiz.ex: Totals: East 400, West 300, North 50. Only East and West exceed 150.

quiz.q:
Table sales:
region | rep | amount
East   | A   | 100
East   | B   | 300
West   | C   | 200
West   | C   | 100
North  | D   | 50

What value does this query return?
SELECT AVG(amount) FROM sales WHERE region = 'East';
What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
opts: WHERE works only on numbers; HAVING works only on text
HAVING filters rows before grouping; WHERE filters groups after
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation
They are identical and can always be swapped
quiz.ex: That is why aggregate conditions such as SUM(amount) > 150 must go in HAVING.

quiz.q:
Table sales:
region | rep | amount
East   | A   | 100
East   | B   | 300
West   | C   | 200
West   | C   | 100
North  | D   | 50

Which query is invalid in standard SQL?
opts: SELECT region, SUM(amount) FROM sales GROUP BY region;
SELECT region, rep, SUM(amount) FROM sales GROUP BY region;
SELECT region, rep, SUM(amount) FROM sales GROUP BY region, rep;
SELECT region, COUNT(*) FROM sales GROUP BY region;
quiz.ex: Every selected column must be grouped or aggregated. rep is neither, and a region can have several reps.

quiz.q:
Table sales:
region | rep | amount
East   | A   | 100
East   | B   | 300
West   | C   | 200
West   | C   | 100
North  | D   | 50

What value does this query return?
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT rep) FROM sales;
quiz.ex: The distinct reps are A, B, C and D (C appears twice but is counted once).

quiz.q: A column email is NULL in 3 of 10 rows. What do COUNT(*) and COUNT(email) return?
opts: 10 and 10
10 and 7
7 and 10
7 and 7
quiz.ex: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) skips NULLs.

chapters.title: Subqueries and CTEs
chapters.read: The subquery and WITH (common table expression) lessons of a free SQL tutorial: scalar subqueries, IN/EXISTS, correlated subqueries, NOT IN and NULL, and breaking a long query into named CTE steps.
chapters.produce: Rewrite three of your earlier multi-step analyses as single queries using CTEs, and write one correlated subquery that finds the top item in each category.

quiz.q:
Table emp:
id | name | dept  | salary
1  | Aiko | Sales | 300
2  | Ben  | Sales | 450
3  | Chen | IT    | 500
4  | Dai  | IT    | 350
5  | Emi  | HR    | 400

How many rows does this query return?
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp);
quiz.ex: Average = (300 + 450 + 500 + 350 + 400) / 5 = 400. Only Ben 450 and Chen 500 are above it.

quiz.q: What is a correlated subquery?
opts: A subquery that runs only once and returns one value
A subquery that refers to a column of the outer query and is logically evaluated once per outer row
A subquery placed in the FROM clause
A query that joins two tables with the same name
quiz.ex: Example: WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE dept = e.dept) depends on the outer row's dept.

quiz.q:
Table emp:
id | name | dept  | salary
1  | Aiko | Sales | 300
2  | Ben  | Sales | 450
3  | Chen | IT    | 500
4  | Dai  | IT    | 350
5  | Emi  | HR    | 400

Which is a valid CTE that lists departments whose total salary is above 500?
opts: SELECT * FROM t WHERE tot > 500 WITH t AS (SELECT dept, SUM(salary) AS tot FROM emp GROUP BY dept);
WITH t AS (SELECT dept, SUM(salary) AS tot FROM emp GROUP BY dept) SELECT * FROM t WHERE tot > 500;
WITH t AS SELECT dept, SUM(salary) AS tot FROM emp GROUP BY dept; SELECT * FROM t WHERE tot > 500;
WITH t (SELECT dept, SUM(salary) FROM emp) WHERE tot > 500;
quiz.ex: A CTE is WITH name AS ( query ) followed by the main query that uses it.

quiz.q:
Table emp:
id | name | dept  | salary
1  | Aiko | Sales | 300
2  | Ben  | Sales | 450
3  | Chen | IT    | 500
4  | Dai  | IT    | 350
5  | Emi  | HR    | 400

How many rows does this query return?
WITH t AS (SELECT dept, SUM(salary) AS tot FROM emp GROUP BY dept)
SELECT * FROM t WHERE tot > 500;
quiz.ex: Totals: Sales 750, IT 850, HR 400. Sales and IT are above 500.

quiz.q: Why can WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT y FROM t) return no rows at all?
opts: If the subquery returns any NULL, every NOT IN comparison becomes unknown; NOT EXISTS avoids this
NOT IN only works with numbers
NOT IN subqueries are limited to 10 values
NOT IN always returns no rows in SQL
quiz.ex: x NOT IN (1, NULL) means x <> 1 AND x <> NULL, and x <> NULL is unknown, so the whole condition is never true.

quiz.q:
Table emp:
id | name | dept  | salary
1  | Aiko | Sales | 300
2  | Ben  | Sales | 450
3  | Chen | IT    | 500
4  | Dai  | IT    | 350
5  | Emi  | HR    | 400

What value does this query return?
SELECT SUM(salary) FROM emp e
WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE dept = e.dept);
quiz.ex: Top earner per department: Sales Ben 450, IT Chen 500, HR Emi 400. 450 + 500 + 400 = 1350.

chapters.title: Window functions
chapters.read: The window function lessons of a free SQL tutorial: OVER, PARTITION BY, ORDER BY inside the window, ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG/LEAD, and running totals and moving averages.
chapters.produce: Using a year of daily prices for one stock (from a free data source) in SQLite, compute the daily return with LAG, a 20-day moving average, and each month's best day with ROW_NUMBER.

quiz.q:
Table scores:
name | team | pts
Ann  | X    | 90
Bob  | X    | 80
Cal  | X    | 80
Dee  | Y    | 70
Eve  | Y    | 95

In SELECT name, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY pts DESC) AS r FROM scores; what is r for Dee?
quiz.ex: Order: Eve 1, Ann 2, Bob and Cal tie at 3, so the next rank skips to 5 for Dee.

quiz.q:
Table scores:
name | team | pts
Ann  | X    | 90
Bob  | X    | 80
Cal  | X    | 80
Dee  | Y    | 70
Eve  | Y    | 95

In SELECT name, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY pts DESC) AS r FROM scores; what is r for Dee?
quiz.ex: DENSE_RANK does not skip after a tie: Eve 1, Ann 2, Bob and Cal 3, Dee 4.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between a window function and GROUP BY?
opts: A window function keeps every input row and adds a calculated value to each; GROUP BY collapses rows into one per group
Window functions can only be used on dates
GROUP BY keeps every row; window functions collapse them
Window functions cannot use aggregates such as SUM
quiz.ex: That is why window functions are used for running totals, ranks and comparisons with the previous row.

quiz.q:
Table scores:
name | team | pts
Ann  | X    | 90
Bob  | X    | 80
Cal  | X    | 80
Dee  | Y    | 70
Eve  | Y    | 95

In SELECT name, SUM(pts) OVER (PARTITION BY team) AS t FROM scores; what is t for Bob?
quiz.ex: Bob is in team X: 90 + 80 + 80 = 250, shown on every team X row.

quiz.q: What does LAG(price) OVER (ORDER BY trade_date) return?
opts: The price from the next row
The lowest price in the table
The average of all earlier prices
The price from the previous row in trade_date order (NULL for the first row)
quiz.ex: LAG looks back; LEAD looks forward. price − LAG(price) gives the daily change.

quiz.q:
Table daily:
day | qty
1   | 5
2   | 3
3   | 7
4   | 2

In SELECT day, SUM(qty) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS run FROM daily; what is run on day 3?
quiz.ex: A running total adds all rows up to the current one: 5 + 3 + 7 = 15.

chapters.title: Excel lookups and pivot tables
chapters.read: Microsoft's free Excel training pages on VLOOKUP, XLOOKUP, INDEX/MATCH, SUMIFS/COUNTIFS, absolute and relative references, and PivotTables.
chapters.produce: Build a workbook that looks up product prices from a master sheet with XLOOKUP and INDEX/MATCH, totals sales with SUMIFS, and summarises the same data with a PivotTable, checking that both totals agree.

quiz.q: In =VLOOKUP(A2, Products!A:C, 3, FALSE), what does FALSE do?
opts: Returns the value from the left of the lookup column
Sorts the table before looking up
Requires an exact match of the lookup value
Returns an approximate match from a sorted list
quiz.ex: FALSE (or 0) means exact match; TRUE or omitted means approximate match, which needs a sorted first column.

quiz.q: What is a well-known limit of VLOOKUP that INDEX/MATCH and XLOOKUP avoid?
opts: VLOOKUP cannot look up text
VLOOKUP works only on one sheet
VLOOKUP cannot return numbers
VLOOKUP can only return a column to the right of the lookup column
quiz.ex: INDEX/MATCH and XLOOKUP take separate lookup and return ranges, so the result can be to the left.

quiz.q:
Cells A2:C4 contain:
A     | B   | C
P-01  | Pen | 120
P-02  | Pad | 300
P-03  | Ink | 80

What does =VLOOKUP("P-02", A2:C4, 3, FALSE) return?
quiz.ex: It finds P-02 in the first column (row 3) and returns the 3rd column of that row: 300.

quiz.q: What is a PivotTable mainly used for?
opts: Encrypting a worksheet
Summarising a data table, e.g. total sales by region and month, without writing formulas
Recording macros
Checking spelling in a worksheet
quiz.ex: Drag fields into rows, columns and values to group and aggregate; refresh when the source data changes.

quiz.q:
Rows 2 to 6 contain:
row | A (region) | B (qty) | C (sales)
2   | East       | 120     | 500
3   | West       | 200     | 800
4   | East       | 80      | 300
5   | East       | 150     | 700
6   | West       | 90      | 400

What does =SUMIFS(C2:C6, A2:A6, "East", B2:B6, ">100") return?
quiz.ex: Rows where region is East and qty > 100 are rows 2 and 5: 500 + 700 = 1200.

quiz.q: A formula in D2 is =B2*$F$1. What happens to $F$1 when the formula is copied down to D3?
opts: It becomes $F$2
It becomes F2 without dollar signs
It stays $F$1, while B2 becomes B3
The formula returns an error
quiz.ex: Dollar signs fix the row and column, so the reference is absolute; B2 is relative and moves with the copy.

chapters.title: A simple 3-statement model in Excel
chapters.read: A free financial modelling tutorial on the three statements: how the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement link through net income, depreciation, working capital, capex, debt and retained earnings, with a balance check.
chapters.produce: Build a 3-year, 3-statement model for a small café in Excel from 10 assumptions (sales growth, margins, capex, depreciation, working capital days, a loan), with a balance check that is zero every year.

quiz.q: How does net income link the three statements?
opts: It is recorded only on the income statement
It is added to cash directly on the balance sheet, skipping the cash flow statement
It reduces total liabilities
It flows into retained earnings on the balance sheet and is the starting line of operating cash flow (indirect method)
quiz.ex: Net income connects the P&L to equity and to the cash flow statement, which then explains the change in cash.

quiz.q: Net income is 100, depreciation 30, accounts receivable increased by 20, and accounts payable increased by 10. What is cash flow from operations (indirect method)?
quiz.ex: 100 + 30 (non-cash) − 20 (more cash tied in receivables) + 10 (more owed to suppliers) = 120.

quiz.q: Opening cash is 200. Cash flow from operations is +120, investing −80 and financing −30. What is closing cash?
Which check proves the balance sheet in a model is consistent?
opts: Net income equals cash flow from operations
Revenue equals total assets
Closing cash equals opening cash
Total assets minus (total liabilities + equity) equals zero in every period
quiz.ex: If the links are right, assets always equal liabilities plus equity; a non-zero check means a broken link.

quiz.q: Opening retained earnings are 500, net income is 100 and dividends paid are 40. What are closing retained earnings?
Where does a capex purchase show up in a 3-statement model?
opts: It increases PP&E on the balance sheet, is a cash outflow in investing activities, and reaches the income statement over time through depreciation
It is an expense on the income statement in full in the year of purchase
It appears only in financing cash flow
It reduces retained earnings directly
quiz.ex: Capex is capitalised, so the P&L sees it gradually as depreciation.

chapters.title: Python with pandas basics
chapters.read: The official pandas getting-started tutorials: DataFrame and Series, read_csv, selecting columns, filtering rows, loc and iloc, groupby, merge, and how missing values (NaN) are handled.
chapters.produce: In a Jupyter notebook, load a CSV of transactions, clean it, and reproduce three earlier SQL results (a filter, a GROUP BY and a LEFT JOIN) in pandas, checking that the numbers match.

quiz.q: Which line loads trades.csv into a DataFrame?
opts: df = pd.DataFrame('trades.csv')
df = pd.load('trades.csv')
df = pd.read_csv('trades.csv')
df = pd.open_csv('trades.csv')
quiz.ex: read_csv parses the file and returns a DataFrame.

quiz.q: Which expression keeps only the rows where amount is greater than 100?
opts: df[df['amount'] > 100]
df['amount' > 100]
df.loc['amount'] > 100
df.filter(amount > 100)
quiz.ex: df['amount'] > 100 builds a True/False Series, and indexing df with it keeps the True rows.

quiz.q:
df = pd.DataFrame({'dept': ['A', 'A', 'B'], 'sal': [100, 200, 300]})
What does df.groupby('dept')['sal'].mean().loc['A'] return?
quiz.ex: Dept A has 100 and 200; the mean is 150.

quiz.q: Which call is the pandas equivalent of a SQL LEFT JOIN on column id?
opts: pd.concat([left, right], how='left')
left.join_left(right, 'id')
pd.merge(left, right, on='id', how='left')
pd.merge(left, right, on='id', how='inner')
quiz.ex: merge with how='left' keeps every row of the left DataFrame and adds matching columns from the right.

quiz.q:
s = pd.Series([3, None, 5])
What does s.mean() return?
quiz.ex: None becomes NaN, and mean() skips NaN by default: (3 + 5) / 2 = 4.

quiz.q: What is the difference between df.loc and df.iloc?
opts: loc is for rows and iloc is for columns
iloc is faster but returns the same thing as loc in every case
loc works only on text data
loc selects by index labels and column names; iloc selects by integer positions
quiz.ex: df.loc[5] is the row whose label is 5; df.iloc[5] is the sixth row by position.

chapters.title: Markets-systems tech: Unix, XML, batch and testing
chapters.read: Free beginner material on the Linux shell (ls, cd, grep, tail, wc, pipes, chmod), XML basics and simple XPath, how end-of-day (EOD) batch processing works in trading systems, and how to write a test plan.
chapters.produce: On a Linux machine or WSL, write a shell one-liner report over a sample batch log (errors per job), parse a small XML trade file with Python, and write a one-page test plan for an EOD batch change.

quiz.q: What does grep "ERROR" eod.log do?
opts: Prints every line of eod.log that contains ERROR
Deletes the lines containing ERROR
Counts the words in eod.log
Renames eod.log to ERROR
quiz.ex: grep searches text for a pattern; add -c to count matching lines or -i to ignore case.

quiz.q:
batch.log contains these 5 lines:
job1,OK
job2,FAIL
job3,OK
job4,FAIL
job5,OK

What number does grep -c FAIL batch.log print?
quiz.ex: -c counts matching lines: job2 and job4 contain FAIL, so 2.

quiz.q: Which snippet is well-formed XML?
opts: <trade id="T1"><notional>1000000</trade></notional>
<trade id=T1><notional>1000000</notional></trade>
<trade id="T1"><notional>1000000</notional>
<trade id="T1"><notional>1000000</notional></trade>
quiz.ex: Tags must be closed and properly nested, and attribute values must be quoted.

quiz.q: What usually happens in a trading system's end-of-day (EOD) batch?
opts: After the market closes, positions are revalued with closing market data, P&L and risk are computed, and reports and downstream feeds are produced
New trades are booked by traders
The trading screens are redesigned
Only user passwords are reset
quiz.ex: EOD is a sequence of dependent jobs (market data load, revaluation, P&L, risk, accounting feeds) run every business day.

quiz.q: Which command shows new lines of a log file as they are written?
opts: tail -f app.log
head app.log
cat -n app.log
wc -l app.log
quiz.ex: tail -f follows the file, which is handy for watching a running batch job.

quiz.q: Which belongs in a test plan?
opts: Only the source code of the system
Scope, approach, test environments, entry and exit criteria, schedule and responsibilities
Only the list of defects found in production
Only the names of the testers
quiz.ex: A test plan says what will be tested, how, where, when, by whom and when testing counts as done.

boss.q:
Table trades:
id | book  | ccy | notional
1  | FX1   | USD | 100
2  | FX1   | EUR | 200
3  | RATES | USD | 300
4  | RATES | USD | 50
5  | EQ    | JPY | 400

Table books:
book   | desk
FX1    | FX
RATES  | Rates
CREDIT | Credit

What value does this query return for the Credit desk?
SELECT b.desk, COUNT(t.id) FROM books b LEFT JOIN trades t ON t.book = b.book GROUP BY b.desk;
boss.ex: CREDIT has no trades, so the LEFT JOIN gives one row with t.id NULL. COUNT(t.id) skips NULL and returns 0 (COUNT(*) would give 1).

boss.q:
Table trades:
id | book  | ccy | notional
1  | FX1   | USD | 100
2  | FX1   | EUR | 200
3  | RATES | USD | 300
4  | RATES | USD | 50
5  | EQ    | JPY | 400

Table books:
book   | desk
FX1    | FX
RATES  | Rates
CREDIT | Credit

What value does this query return?
SELECT SUM(notional) FROM trades WHERE book NOT IN (SELECT book FROM books);
boss.ex: Only book EQ is missing from books (and books has no NULLs), so the sum is trade 5's 400.

boss.q:
Table trades:
id | book  | ccy | notional
1  | FX1   | USD | 100
2  | FX1   | EUR | 200
3  | RATES | USD | 300
4  | RATES | USD | 50
5  | EQ    | JPY | 400

Table books:
book   | desk
FX1    | FX
RATES  | Rates
CREDIT | Credit

What value does this query return?
WITH r AS (SELECT book, notional, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY book ORDER BY notional DESC) AS rn FROM trades)
SELECT SUM(notional) FROM r WHERE rn = 1;
boss.ex: Largest trade per book: FX1 200, RATES 300, EQ 400. 200 + 300 + 400 = 900.

boss.q:
Table emp:
id | name | dept  | salary
1  | Aiko | Sales | 300
2  | Ben  | Sales | 450
3  | Chen | IT    | 500
4  | Dai  | IT    | 350
5  | Emi  | HR    | 400

Which query returns the second-highest salary?
opts: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary > (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp);
SELECT salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary ASC LIMIT 1;
SELECT MIN(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp);
SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp);
boss.ex: Excluding the top salary (500) and taking the max of the rest gives 450.

boss.q:
Table trades:
id | book  | ccy | notional

Which formula returns the price in column C for product code P-07 found in column A, using an exact match?
opts: =INDEX(A2:A10, MATCH("P-07", C2:C10, 0))
=INDEX(C2:C10, MATCH("P-07", A2:A10, 0))
=INDEX(C2:C10, MATCH("P-07", A2:A10, 1))
boss.ex: MATCH with 0 finds the exact position of P-07 in column A, and INDEX returns the value at that position in column C.

boss.q: A company has net income 80, depreciation 20, an inventory increase of 15, a decrease in accounts payable of 5, capex of 60, debt repayment of 10 and opening cash of 100. What is closing cash?
Which pandas code is closest to SQL's GROUP BY book HAVING SUM(notional) > 250, returning the original rows of those books?
opts: df[df['notional'] > 250].groupby('book')
df.groupby('book').filter(lambda g: g['notional'].sum() > 250)
df.groupby('book')['notional'].sum() > 250
df.sort_values('notional').head(250)
boss.ex: groupby().filter() keeps or drops whole groups based on a group-level condition, like HAVING. The third option only gives True/False per book.

boss.q:
What does this pipeline output?
grep FAIL batch.log | cut -d',' -f2 | sort | uniq -c
opts: The total number of lines in batch.log
The FAIL lines sorted by their first field, with duplicates removed
For lines containing FAIL, the count of each distinct value in the second comma-separated field
The second field of every line, including those without FAIL
boss.ex: grep keeps FAIL lines, cut takes field 2, sort groups equal values, and uniq -c counts each run of equal values.
